Tribulation
trib-yoo-LAY-shun
noun / doctrine
From the Latin tribulatio, “a pressing, an affliction”; the doctrine of the afflictions through which God brings His people into His kingdom.

See also: Tribulation

📖 Biblical Definition

Tribulation is the doctrine of the afflictions through which God appoints His people to pass on their way to glory. It is no accident of the Christian life but its very road: Paul and Barnabas confirmed the souls of the disciples, “exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22). The Lord warned His own plainly, yet comforted them in the same breath: “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Joh 16:33). Far from being a sign of God’s displeasure, tribulation is the furnace in which He works the graces of His people: “tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope” (Rom 5:3–5). And in the great vision of heaven, the redeemed multitude is named as those “which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). Thus the church is taught to expect affliction, not to be surprised by it as though some strange thing happened, but to count it the appointed path. Through tribulation God conforms His people to Christ, who Himself entered His glory through suffering; and the same tribulation that presses them now is working a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. The kingdom is entered through the cross, never around it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that God brings His people into His kingdom through much affliction, conformed to the suffering Christ.

TRIBULATION, the afflictions through which God brings His people to glory.

We must through much tribulation enter the kingdom of God (Act 14:22).

In the world the saints have tribulation, but Christ has overcome it (Joh 16:33).

Tribulation worketh patience, experience, and hope (Rom 5:3–5).

The redeemed come out of great tribulation, robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 7:14).

📖 Key Scripture

Act 14:22 — "Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God."

Joh 16:33 — "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

Rom 5:3 — "And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;"

Rev 7:14 — "And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Dispensational pre-tribulation escapism corrupts the doctrine of tribulation, promising the church a secret exit from affliction by way of a 19th-century novelty.

expand to see more

The live corruption is dispensational pre-tribulation escapism, which teaches that the church will be secretly raptured away before a coming great tribulation, so that the saints are promised an exit from affliction rather than a passage through it. This rests upon dispensational premillennialism, a system unknown to the church for eighteen centuries, devised in the nineteenth by John Nelson Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible. No Reformation confession contains it; it is a novelty, not the faith once delivered. The dictionary rejects it as the voice-lock requires, naming it for what it is: a recent invention superimposed upon the plain teaching that “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22).

The error is not merely chronological but pastoral and deadly. It teaches the church to expect escape where Christ taught her to expect affliction: “In the world ye shall have tribulation” (Joh 16:33). It cannot account for the great multitude in heaven who “came out of great tribulation” (Rev 7:14), nor for the apostles who endured it, nor for the suffering church in every age and land. By promising an exit, it leaves believers unprepared to suffer and tempts them to count affliction a sign that something has gone wrong. The dictionary holds the historic faith: the kingdom is entered through the cross, tribulation is the appointed path, and God uses it to work patience, experience, and hope in His people, conforming them to the Christ who Himself entered glory through suffering.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

God brings His people into the kingdom through much affliction, conforming them to the suffering Christ.

expand to see more

Tribulatio — Latin, “a pressing, an affliction.”

The road — through much tribulation into the kingdom (Act 14:22).

Comfort — Christ has overcome the world (Joh 16:33).

Fruit — tribulation worketh patience and hope (Rom 5:3–5).

The robed multitude — come out of great tribulation (Rev 7:14).

Usage

"Expect affliction as the appointed path; be not surprised as though some strange thing happened."

"Tribulation is the furnace in which God works patience, experience, and hope in His people."

"The kingdom is entered through the cross, never around it; seek no secret exit from suffering."
